contracts.grain: One row per claim (open, reopened, or closed within the last 90 days) whose incurred amount (paid to date plus latest outstanding reserve) is at least EUR 25,000 as at the as-of date.

columns.name: claim_status
columns.description: Trimmed and upper-cased from the source status.

columns.name: incurred_amount
columns.description: paid_to_date + outstanding_reserve as at as_of_date; always >= 25000.

columns.name: incurred_90d_ago
columns.description: Paid to date plus latest reserve as at as_of_date minus 90 days.

columns.name: reserve_changes_90d
columns.description: Count of reserve records dated within the last 90 days.

columns.name: days_since_last_activity
columns.description: Days from the later of the last keyed payment date or last reserve date to as_of_date; NULL if there was no activity.

columns.name: watch_category
columns.description: NEW if incurred_90d_ago < 25000; DETERIORATING if up more than 10%; IMPROVING if down more than 10%; else STABLE.

cases.description: Claims with mixed-case CLOSED statuses ('Closed', 'closed', 'clOSed') closed more than 90 days before AsOfDate (PriorDate = 2025-10-02). Under the CI collation, `status <> 'CLOSED'` is false for these rows, so the legacy job drops them. A binary Spark comparison would keep them. There are also controls: an OPEN claim, an upper-case CLOSED claim closed long ago (dropped by both), and a 'Closed' claim closed recently (kept by both). Every claim has a EUR 50,000 reserve, so any claim that passes the filter is written to the output.

Claims whose raw status has trailing spaces ('CLOSED ', 'CLOSED  ') and was closed before PriorDate 2025-10-02. SQL Server ignores trailing spaces when comparing, so these count as CLOSED and are dropped. A Spark comparison of the untrimmed string would keep them. Controls: an OPEN claim, an 'OPEN ' claim with padding (kept either way), an unpadded CLOSED claim closed long ago (dropped by both), and a padded 'CLOSED ' claim closed recently (kept). Every claim has a EUR 60,000 reserve.

The last-activity choice with NULL on either side. Claims are set up with payments only (last_reserve_date is NULL), reserves only (last_payment_date is NULL), a later payment than reserve, a later reserve than payment, and a NULL-amount payment that does not count as activity, so last_payment_date stays NULL even though a payment row is dated later. In the legacy job, ISNULL(..., '19000101') becomes the date 1900-01-01. A naive coalesce with the string literal would turn the comparison into a string comparison or a cast failure, which changes which date is picked or turns days_since_last_activity into NULL. Every claim's incurred amount is at least EUR 25,000.

Claims whose last activity falls at different distances before AsOfDate 2025-12-31: on AsOfDate itself, one day before, mid-month, across a year boundary (2024-01-15), and one where the latest payment is dated after AsOfDate and so is excluded. The legacy DATEDIFF(DAY, last_activity, AsOfDate) is positive. A Spark datediff with the arguments left in T-SQL order would return negative values.

Claims whose incurred amount is exactly 1.10x or 0.90x of incurred_90d_ago. A reserve on 2025-09-01 sets the prior amount and a reserve on 2025-12-01 sets the current amount. Pairs: 25000.10→27500.11, 30000.00→33000.00, 33333.30→36666.63 (all exactly 1.10x), and 30000.30→27000.27, 28000.70→25200.63, 33333.30→29999.97 (all exactly 0.90x). With exact DECIMAL arithmetic the strict > and < fail, so the legacy job marks these STABLE. Double literals can push them into DETERIORATING or IMPROVING. A clear DETERIORATING claim (40000→50000) is included as a control.
